title: A Viability Event in the Prospectus: Why the AT1 Write-Down Was Contractual, and What That Does Not Settle

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The yield was the compensation for exactly this. FINMA describes what the instruments are: AT1 capital "designed in such a way that they are written down or converted into Common Equity Tier 1 capital before the equity capital of the bank concerned is completely used up or written down", and "mainly held by institutional investors due to their risk profile and large denominations". The release lists thirteen publicly issued instruments by ISIN, running from a 7.500% note issued in December 2013 to a 9.750% issue of June 2022 — coupons that were the price of the clause that destroyed them.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The trigger was written in before the crisis and it was broad. The instruments "contractually provide that they will be completely written down in a ‘Viability Event’, in particular if extraordinary government support is granted." A clause triggered by rescue is a clause that fires precisely when the holder most expects protection.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog here was not in the documents but in the expectation around them. FINMA had to publish this release at all because of "numerous enquiries", four days after the event, to explain a basis that was already in the prospectuses the holders had bought. The hierarchy people believed they held was not the hierarchy the contract described.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The write-down removed a class of liability from the balance sheet being handed to the acquirer. FINMA records the date the condition was met: "Credit Suisse was granted extraordinary liquidity assistance loans secured by a federal default guarantee on 19 March 2023", and that the Federal Council enacted its Emergency Ordinance the same day, which "also authorises FINMA to order the borrower and the financial group to write down Additional Tier 1 capital."
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The containment was an emergency ordinance enacted on the day it was needed, layered on top of a contractual clause — belt and braces for a decision taken over a weekend. FINMA's own account cites both: it "relies on the issuance prospectuses for the bonds and the Federal Council’s Emergency Ordinance". Tier 2 bonds were not written down. What this document is not is a court ruling; bondholder litigation is not addressed in it and no outcome is asserted here.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The post-2008 bail-in architecture: loss-absorbing capital sold to institutional investors on the premise that it converts or writes down before taxpayers are touched.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: A worked precedent that a viability clause can fire on the granting of state liquidity support, and an emergency ordinance giving the supervisor express power to order the write-down — enacted the same day the support was granted.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The instruments paid a high coupon because of the write-down clause; the clause existed so that the state would not have to pay; the state support was itself the event that triggered the clause.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That Switzerland tore up the capital hierarchy overnight — wiping out $17 billion of bondholders while shareholders got paid — and invented the legal basis for it afterwards.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The basis was in the documents the bondholders bought. FINMA states that the instruments "contractually provide that they will be completely written down in a ‘Viability Event’, in particular if extraordinary government support is granted", and that the condition was met when Credit Suisse received "extraordinary liquidity assistance loans secured by a federal default guarantee on 19 March 2023". The Emergency Ordinance of the same day was additional authority, not the sole basis: FINMA says it relies on both "the issuance prospectuses for the bonds and the Federal Council’s Emergency Ordinance". AT1 is also designed to absorb loss ahead of equity being fully written down, which the release states expressly. But this dossier should not take the regulator's account as the last word either: the document read here is FINMA explaining its own decision four days afterwards, not a court testing it, and bondholder litigation is outside what was read. The precise, defensible statement is that the write-down had a stated contractual and statutory basis, not that its lawfulness was adjudicated.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: A FINMA release of 23 March 2023 explaining the basis for the complete write-down of Credit Suisse AT1 instruments, resting on the issuance prospectuses and the Federal Council’s Emergency Ordinance. The contractual trigger: complete write-down in a Viability Event, in particular where extraordinary government support is granted. The triggering fact: extraordinary liquidity assistance loans secured by a federal default guarantee on 19 March 2023. The Emergency Ordinance of 19 March 2023 authorising FINMA to order the write-down. Tier 2 bonds not written down. Thirteen affected publicly issued instruments listed by ISIN, issue date, currency and coupon. And the design principle stated by the regulator: AT1 is written down or converted before the bank’s equity capital is completely used up.

citations.title: Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority (FINMA), "FINMA provides information about the basis for writing down AT1 capital instruments", press release, 23 March 2023
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full from FINMA's own site. The release exists to answer the objection: "The Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority FINMA hereby explains the basis for the complete write-down of the nominal value of AT1 capital instruments issued by Credit Suisse. For this, FINMA relies on the issuance prospectuses for the bonds and the Federal Council’s Emergency Ordinance." And: "FINMA has instructed Credit Suisse to completely write down its AT1 instruments and to inform the bondholders concerned without delay. Tier 2 bonds are not written down." THE CONTRACTUAL BASIS, which is the answer to the claim that the hierarchy was inverted lawlessly: "The AT1 instruments issued by Credit Suisse contractually provide that they will be completely written down in a ‘Viability Event’, in particular if extraordinary government support is granted. As Credit Suisse was granted extraordinary liquidity assistance loans secured by a federal default guarantee on 19 March 2023, these contractual conditions were met for the AT1 instruments issued by the bank." THE ORDINANCE: "On 19 March 2023, the Federal Council enacted the Emergency Ordinance on Additional Liquidity Assistance Loans and the Granting of Federal Default Guarantees for Liquidity Assistance Loans by the Swiss National Bank to Systemically Important Banks. The Ordinance also authorises FINMA to order the borrower and the financial group to write down Additional Tier 1 capital." ON WHAT THE INSTRUMENTS ARE FOR: "AT1 instruments in Switzerland are designed in such a way that they are written down or converted into Common Equity Tier 1 capital before the equity capital of the bank concerned is completely used up or written down. The instruments publicly issued by large banks are mainly held by institutional investors due to their risk profile and large denominations." The release then lists every affected publicly issued instrument by ISIN, issue date, currency and coupon — thirteen entries beginning with 7.500% Tier 1 Capital Notes issued 11 December 2013 and running to a 9.750% issue of 23 June 2022. FINMA CEO Urban Angehrn is quoted on the wider resolution: "On Sunday, a solution could be found to protect clients, the financial centre and the markets." This is the regulator's own statement of its legal basis, published four days after the event. It is not a court ruling, and litigation by bondholders is not addressed in it.
